h.en: Types of Requirements: Functional and Non-Functional

body.en:
• Functional requirements: the verbs of the system - what it must DO. 'Student books a seat', 'system prints a receipt', 'admin cancels a route'. Every one can be tested.
  • Non-functional requirements (quality attributes/constraints): how WELL and under WHAT limits - response under 2 seconds, 1000 concurrent users, encrypted passwords, Hindi+Gujarati UI, budget cap.
  • Common exam framing: functional = service statement; non-functional = quality/constraint statement (performance, security, reliability, usability, portability).
  • Both belong in the SRS; a system with perfect features but 30-second replies is still a failed project.

• Interviews: structured 1-to-1 talks with key users - deep but slow.
  • Questionnaires/surveys: collect from MANY users fast and cheap; quality limited by question quality.
  • Brainstorming/workshops (JAD): stakeholders solve requirements together - conflicts settle in the room.
  • Observation: watch users work; uncovers steps nobody REMEMBERS to mention.
  • Document analysis: study existing forms, registers and reports for data definitions.
  • Prototyping: a quick mock makes vague wishes concrete (Unit 1).
  • Practice (Practical 4): blend techniques - interview the registrar, questionnaire the students, watch the counter clerks.

h.en: SRS: What It Is and Its Structure

body.en:
• The SRS is the negotiated contract between customer and developers recording exactly what the software must do - prepared after requirement gathering (Practical 5 is a broad SRS for your project).
  • Typical IEEE-style structure: 1. Introduction (purpose, scope, definitions), 2. Overall description (product perspective, users, constraints, assumptions), 3. Specific requirements (functional + non-functional + interfaces), appendices.
  • Distinguish voices: customer requirements are the client's plain-language wishes ('a fast bus booking'); functional requirements are testable system actions ('the system shall confirm a seat within 2 seconds').
  • The SRS is a legal-ish document: ambiguity is a defect.

• Correct - every requirement stated is one the client truly needs.
  • Unambiguous - every sentence has exactly ONE interpretation (the flagship exam answer: two developers must not be able to build two systems).
  • Complete - nothing significant left blank (including what happens on bad input).
  • Consistent - requirements never contradict each other.
  • Ranked for importance/stability - MUST vs nice-to-have flagged.
  • Verifiable - each item testable ('fast' fails this test; 'under 2 s at 500 users' passes).
  • Modifiable, traceable - changes are absorbed cleanly; each requirement can be traced from SRS to design to test case.

h.en: Good Design and Analysis vs Design

body.en:
• Analysis answers WHAT (needs, use cases); design answers HOW (modules, classes, data structures, interfaces, algorithms). Analysis talks to the customer; design instructs the builders.
  • Characteristics of a GOOD design: correct (does the job per SRS), complete, efficient, understandable, and above all changeable - because requirements WILL change.
  • Changeability is achieved through modular design, where two measures rule every choice: cohesion and coupling.

• Cohesion = how strongly the items inside one module belong together. HIGHER is better.
  • Worst→best ladder: coincidental (random grab-bag) < logical (similar kind: 'all print utilities') < temporal (done at the same time: 'init stuff') < procedural (fixed sequence) < communicational (work on the same data) < sequential (one step's output feeds the next) < functional (every line serves ONE clear task - the goal).
  • Memory anchor: C-L-T-P-C-S-F climbing to functional.
  • Rule in practice: if a module's name needs 'and' ("validates and saves and prints"), split it.

• Coupling = how much one module depends on another. LOWER is better.
  • Worst→best: content (one module rewrites another's insides) > common (shared global data) > external (shared file format/protocol) > control (flags steering another's logic) > stamp (whole records handed over when a field or two would do) > data (just needed parameters) > message (talk only through messages/events - loosest).
  • Why you care: high coupling makes edits ripple through the system - one change in a global structure rewrites five modules' logic.
  • The design mantra for the exam and for life: high cohesion + low coupling.

• A DFD shows how data MOVES through a system - the four symbols: process (circle, transforms data), external entity (rectangle: outside actor), data store (two parallel lines: file/DB at rest), data flow (labeled arrow).
  • Rules that exams check: data always flows THROUGH a process; entities never talk directly to each other or to stores; every flow is labeled; every process both consumes and produces data.
  • DFDs document the business workflow without deciding HOW it is coded - they are analysis artifacts handed to design.

• Context level: the ENTIRE system as a single bubble, with only external entities and the flows between them - 'the system at a glance'.
  • Level 1: explode that bubble into its major functions (4-8 bubbles), keeping the same external flows - an act called balancing (in/out flows must match between levels).
  • Deeper levels keep exploding: bubble 2 becomes 2.1, 2.2, ... Stop when a bubble is one clear task.
  • Practical 6: build context + level-1 DFD for your chosen project (here: food ordering) and note the order store under the bubbles.

• A use-case diagram is the who-wants-what map: stick-figure actors (roles, not persons) linked to use case ovals inside a system-boundary rectangle.
  • Relations: default plain lines ('actor can do this'); <<include>> when one case always reuses another (place order → include pay); <<extend>> for optional add-ons (apply coupon).
  • Practical 7: derive actors first, then per-actor goals - each oval is a testable user goal, not a screen.

• The static backbone: classes as three-compartment boxes (name / attributes / operations), with associations (plain line, e.g. Member borrows Book), multiplicity (1, 0..*, 1..*), and generalisation (hollow triangle toward the parent: EBook → Book IS-A).
  • Also know: aggregation (hollow diamond - weak whole-part), composition (filled diamond - strong), dependency (dashed arrow).
  • Build order (Practical 8): nouns of the SRS → classes; their properties → attributes; verbs → operations; relationships + multiplicity last.

• Shows the physical packaging: components (replaceable boxes such as OrderService, PaymentGateway) with interfaces drawn as lollipop (provided) and socket (required).
  • Components connect only through interfaces - so a payment-gateway swap touches nothing else.
  • Practical 9: carve your app into 3-5 components and mark what each OFFERS and what it NEEDS.

• An interaction over time: objects/actors across the top with vertical dashed lifelines running downward; horizontal solid arrows are calls, dashed arrows returns; thin bars on lifelines show activation.
  • Time flows DOWN the page, so the diagram doubles as the call script for one scenario (e.g. place an order with a payment gateway).
  • Practical 10: pick ONE use case and lay out its message order - if the diagram reads cleanly, the workflow is understood.

• Flowchart's object-aware cousin: filled dot = start, ringed dot = end, rounded boxes = actions, diamonds = decisions, bold fork/join bars = parallel work (e.g. notify kitchen WHILE the receipt prints).
  • Swimlanes can assign actions to roles (customer lane vs kitchen lane) - great for showing hand-offs.
  • Practical 11: draw the complete flow of one user story, marking where the flow splits on 'pay online?' and where it merges back.

q.en: What are functional requirements?

a.en: Statements of what the system DOES - services like booking a seat, issuing a receipt, searching records.

q.en: What are non-functional requirements?

a.en: Quality and constraint statements - performance, security, capacity, usability, portability - telling how well functions must work.

q.en: Give one functional and one non-functional requirement for a library system.

a.en: Functional: 'the system records each book issue'; Non-functional: 'search results appear within 2 seconds for 200 users.'

q.en: Name four requirement gathering techniques.

a.en: Interviews, questionnaires, brainstorming workshops and observation (plus document study and prototyping).

q.en: When is observation better than interviews?

a.en: When users do work they cannot fully describe - watching reveals steps never mentioned in a talk.

q.en: What is requirement analysis?

a.en: Classifying, negotiating and validating gathered requirements into a consistent, agreed set before designing.

q.en: What is an SRS?

a.en: Software Requirement Specification - the formal document stating exactly what the software must do, agreed between customer and developer.

q.en: List any four characteristics of a good SRS.

a.en: Correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent (also: ranked, verifiable, modifiable, traceable).

q.en: Why must an SRS be unambiguous?

a.en: Every sentence needs exactly ONE meaning - ambiguity lets two developers build two different systems from the same line.

q.en: Customer requirements vs functional requirements?

a.en: Customer requirements are the client's plain-language needs; functional requirements are their testable restatement as system actions.

q.en: What makes a requirement 'verifiable'?

a.en: Some finite, cost-effective test exists to prove the system meets it ('responds within 2 s' - yes; 'fast' - no).

q.en: Analysis vs design, one line?

a.en: Analysis defines WHAT the system must do for users; design defines HOW the build will do it for the developers.

q.en: What makes a design 'good'?

a.en: Correct, complete, efficient, understandable and - above all - changeable.

q.en: Define cohesion.

a.en: The measure of how strongly the elements INSIDE one module belong together - the higher, the better.

q.en: Best and worst cohesion types?

a.en: Best: functional (one clear job). Worst: coincidental (a random grab-bag).

q.en: Define coupling.

a.en: The measure of interdependence BETWEEN modules - the lower, the better.

q.en: Worst and best coupling types?

a.en: Worst: content coupling (one rewrites another's innards). Best: message/data coupling (only needed parameters/messages cross).

q.en: State the design golden rule.

a.en: High cohesion, low coupling - modules each do one clear job and lean on each other as little as possible.

q.en: What is a DFD?

a.en: Data Flow Diagram - shows how data moves through processes, stores and external entities, without fixing code details.

q.en: Name the four DFD symbols.

a.en: Process (circle), external entity (rectangle), data store (two parallel lines), data flow (labeled arrow).

q.en: What is a context-level DFD?

a.en: The whole system drawn as ONE bubble with only external entities and the flows between them.

q.en: What changes from context to level-1 DFD?

a.en: The single bubble is exploded into 4-8 major functions; external flows must stay balanced across the change.

q.en: What is balancing in a DFD?

a.en: The in/out flows of a bubble on one level must exactly match the in/out flows of its expanded lower level.

q.en: Can a data store talk directly to an entity?

a.en: No - all data movement passes through a process bubble; that's a DFD rule commonly probed.

q.en: What does a use case diagram show?

a.en: Actors (roles) and the user goals (use cases) they can perform within the system boundary.

q.en: include vs extend in use cases?

a.en: <<include>> = always-reused shared part; <<extend>> = optional behaviour added only in some cases.

q.en: What are the three compartments of a class box?

a.en: Class name, attributes, operations.

q.en: What does multiplicity mean in a class diagram?

a.en: The count constraint at each end of an association - e.g. Member 1...* borrows Book 0...*.

q.en: Association vs generalisation?

a.en: Association links peer classes (borrows); generalisation is IS-A inheritance (EBook -> Book, hollow triangle).

q.en: What does a component diagram emphasise?

a.en: Physical, replaceable units (components) and the provided/required interfaces they snap together through.

q.en: Lollipop vs socket symbols?

a.en: Lollipop = PROVIDED interface (offered service); socket = REQUIRED interface (needed service).

q.en: What does a sequence diagram show?

a.en: Interaction over time: objects across the top, lifelines downward, ordered messages (calls solid, returns dashed).

q.en: When do you pick a sequence diagram?

a.en: To walk one scenario step by step in time order - e.g. exactly what happens when the student taps 'order'.

q.en: Sequence vs activity diagram?

a.en: Sequence emphasises WHO sends WHICH message WHEN; activity emphasises flow of actions including decisions and parallel branches.

q.en: What are the start and end symbols in an activity diagram?

a.en: A filled circle; a bull's-eye (ring with filled dot).

q.en: What are swimlanes for?

a.en: They group actions by the actor/system-role that performs them, making hand-offs visible.

q.en: Subject verbs for UML: which diagram for 'workflow with decisions'?

a.en: Activity diagram.

q.en: Practical 6: give a sensible level-1 bubble list for a food app.

a.en: browse menu, place order, pay, notify kitchen.

q.en: Which SIX artifacts does Practical 4-11 ask you to produce?

a.en: Gathered requirements, a broad SRS, DFD + E-R diagrams, use-case diagram, class/component/sequence/activity diagrams.

q.en: What draws biggest exam marks from this unit?

a.en: DFD levels, cohesion/coupling ladders and each UML diagram symbol set - draw them.

q.en: Why does a class diagram matter before coding?

a.en: It freezes the nouns, their data and relations, so implementation follows one agreed static structure.
